name: Lakshamma
definition: Lakshamma is a composite portrait of a Soliga woman juggling flower vending and farm labour in Yelandur taluk, Chamarajanagara district, navigating seasonal work, tribal identity and the challenges of raising children in a remote, drought-prone landscape. She represents many in Chamarajanagara's tribal hamlets who straddle forest-linked livelihoods, wage work and persistent questions of land rights, school access and health reach.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Lakshamma rises before dawn most days to walk three kilometres to the weekly market in Yelandur town, carrying a basket of jasmine and marigold she buys from a local grower near Kollegal. She sells flowers to temple-goers and wedding planners, earning between three hundred and six hundred rupees on a good market day. Outside market days she works as a daily-wage farmhand weeding ragi and cotton fields, paid one hundred and eighty to two hundred rupees for seven hours under the sun. The work is irregular—Yelandur's rainfed agriculture offers fewer days than the canal-fed tracts near Mysuru, and drought declarations mean even fewer. Her husband migrates seasonally to coffee estates in Kodagu and Chikkamagaluru, sending home two to three thousand rupees a month when work is available. The household's income is precarious: flower sales fluctuate with festivals and weddings, farm wages dry up between sowing and harvest, and her husband's remittances are unpredictable. They own a small plot of dry land near the forest fringe, but lack a clear patta and have been unable to access bank credit. Economic pressure is constant; every illness or school expense forces a reckoning.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Lakshamma lives with her husband, three children—two daughters aged fifteen and twelve, and a son aged nine—and her aging mother-in-law in a thatched house on the edge of their hamlet, twenty minutes' walk from the paved road. Her husband is away for eight months of the year; she shoulders most daily decisions, from rationing rice to managing the children's schooling. Her elder daughter helps with cooking, fetching water from the hand pump and caring for her grandmother, whose arthritis has worsened. The family's Soliga identity shapes their social ties—most neighbors are kin or clan members, and they observe Male Mahadeshwara worship and forest-linked festivals. Gender roles are traditional but flexible by necessity: Lakshamma manages money, negotiates with flower buyers and deals with the anganwadi and school, tasks her mother-in-law says were once men's domain. Marriage happened early for her—she was sixteen—and she worries her elder daughter will face the same pressure, despite her own determination to keep the girl in school. The household is close-knit but stretched; caregiving, earning and managing fall mostly on her.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Lakshamma herself attended school only until Class 5; the nearest higher primary was too far, and her parents needed her labour. Her two daughters study at the government Kannada-medium school in the hamlet—the elder in Class 10, the younger in Class 7—and her son is in Class 4. The school runs until Class 10 but has only three teachers for over eighty children across all grades, and the headmaster post has been vacant for two years. Her elder daughter travels five kilometres by KSRTC bus under the Shakti scheme to attend bridge classes in Yelandur town, preparing for the SSLC exam; the free travel has been a relief, but the girl still misses days when household work piles up or the bus breaks down. Lakshamma dreams her daughters will finish SSLC and perhaps join a nursing course or government job, escaping the wage-labour cycle. The school provides midday meals and uniforms, but notebooks, pens and exam fees stretch the household budget. Her son is bright, but she worries his teachers don't push him. The Adichunchanagiri Mutt runs a residential school for tribal children in Chamarajanagara town, and neighbors have urged her to send her younger daughter there, but she is reluctant to part with her. Education is both hope and a daily struggle.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: The nearest primary health centre is in Yelandur town, an hour's walk or a fifteen-rupee auto ride away. Lakshamma's mother-in-law suffers from joint pain and high blood pressure, but the PHC rarely has the BP medication in stock, forcing them to buy it at a private pharmacy in town for a hundred and twenty rupees a strip. Lakshamma herself has chronic anaemia—diagnosed during a health camp two years ago—but she rarely takes the iron tablets because they upset her stomach and she can't afford to lose a day's work. Her children have been vaccinated at the anganwadi, but her son had a bout of fever and diarrhoea last monsoon that required two days at the Chamarajanagara district hospital, costing the family nearly three thousand rupees in transport, tests and medicines. Malnutrition and anaemia are common among children in the hamlet; the anganwadi worker distributes take-home rations, but the quantities are small. Access to safe drinking water is a worry—the hand pump sometimes runs dry, and during summer they fetch water from a borewell a kilometre away. Healthcare means lost wages, travel costs and uncertain outcomes; serious illness is a family crisis.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Lakshamma's Soliga identity is central to her life. The hamlet's social fabric is woven from kinship, shared labour and forest ties—families gather honey and tamarind from the forest fringe, though the BRT tiger reserve buffer restrictions have tightened access in recent years. The community observes Male Mahadeshwara Swamy's festival at MM Hills with an annual pilgrimage, and Lakshamma saves for months to make the journey with her children. The Soliga language is spoken at home and among neighbors, though her children learn Kannada at school and are beginning to shift. The hamlet has no formal caste hierarchy, but interactions with non-Soliga landlords and flower buyers often carry an undertone of condescension. Lakshamma participates in a women's self-help group organized by an NGO working with tribal communities; it meets monthly and has helped her save small sums, though she has not yet taken a loan. Trust and reciprocity within the hamlet are strong; outside it, she navigates a world where her tribal identity often means being overlooked or spoken down to.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Lakshamma's household receives ten kilograms of rice per person per month under Anna Bhagya, collected from the ration shop in Yelandur town; the shopkeeper sometimes shortchanges the weight, but complaining feels risky. She has a voter ID and votes in every election—her hamlet is a polling booth—but she feels politicians visit only during campaigns and forget them afterward. Her husband worked under MGNREGA for forty days last year, earning a little over seven thousand rupees, but the work dried up and payment was delayed. The family has applied for a land patta under the Forest Rights Act, with help from the NGO, but the application has been pending for three years without explanation. The anganwadi worker is helpful but overstretched, covering three hamlets. Lakshamma has heard of the Aspirational District program for Chamarajanagara and seen district officials visit the school during a health camp, but no tangible change has followed. The local gram panchayat member is from a non-Soliga community and rarely consults the hamlet. She sees government schemes as essential—ration, Shakti, school meals—but their reach is patchy, their implementation indifferent, and the tribal community's voice weak. Politics feels distant; survival is immediate.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Lakshamma worries most about her daughters' futures—whether they will finish school, avoid early marriage and find work that offers dignity and security. She is proud of her Soliga heritage and Male Mahadeshwara worship, but she also resents that her community is seen as backward or in need of rescue rather than respect. She blames the forest department for restricting access to honey and minor forest produce that once supplemented income, and she blames the education and health systems for being absent when most needed. She wishes her husband could find steady work closer to home so the family wouldn't be split for months on end. She takes pride in managing the household alone, in sending her children to school and in saving a few hundred rupees each month in the SHG, small victories against relentless pressure. She demands better teachers, a PHC with reliable medicine stocks, land rights that are honored, not just promised, and recognition that tribal families like hers are not charity cases but citizens. Her worldview is grounded in the daily calculus of survival, the fierce love for her children, and a quiet, persistent anger that Chamarajanagara, and Yelandur especially, are always last in line.
